title: The Chaos in AI Evaluation Is Not a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
dek: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
why: This episode has medium information density, but the first half's first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI moved from chaos to discipline has direct reference value for anyone building medical AI products.
who: Engineers and founders working on medical AI products, clinical validation, or regulatory submissions, and researchers interested in how evidence standards for medical AI get established.
skip: The personal background segment in the lightning round (first job, favorite paper) can be skipped.

points.h: Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up to scrutiny
points.body: Around 2019, new papers every week claimed "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," but these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down drastically — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best-performing models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

points.h: Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
points.body: CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially checklists specifying which items must be reported in a paper. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it反过来 forces methodological rigor to rise, though that's hard to measure.

points.h: Guidelines are produced by Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
points.body: CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a set of candidate items proposed through literature review and expert opinion, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that can't reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu said doing this kind of consensus project well takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multi-round participation, you can't skimp on time or reach.

points.h: Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fiercely debated
points.body: Andy Beam recalled that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner stood up on the small stage and said "No, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That debate was later commissioned into a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most-cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly took the "no" side in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the end, which is ultimately just beneficial effects.

points.h: Being a regulatory consultant without industry experience felt insincere
points.body: At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting felt a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She said Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year, she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

points.h: Short term, computer scientists set direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
points.body: Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what "driven" means, and after confirming it meant "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is — the people who process data, choose metrics, and choose benchmarks determine which direction progress goes in the short term; but if the endpoint is truly being used on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

points.h: Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
points.body: Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond, and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models continue advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being a "companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, maybe recovery, maybe not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

points.h: Most optimistic is dismantling old medical concepts; most pessimistic is we dare not
points.body: Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gave her PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, rigidly sticking to evaluation methods and guidelines from the past ten or twenty years during a period of new technological change, missing opportunities for discovery.

terms.def: Multiple rounds of anonymous voting plus in-person discussion, used to reach consensus among experts on which items matter.
An international checklist of what must be reported in randomized controlled trial papers; the AI version is CONSORT AI.
A reporting checklist for clinical trial protocol papers; the AI version is SPIRIT AI.
A loose umbrella term for a group of inflammatory eye diseases that show white dots in the fundus, possibly driven by different mechanisms.
